query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures (300–600 °C), the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by the formation of a transient, nanocrystalline oxide layer at the coating surface, which enhances wear resistance through self-lubrication and surface hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a fine-grained microstructure on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (or controlled diffusion treatment) to deliberately form a stabilized nanocrystalline oxide layer on the coating surface prior to high-temperature wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted in the range of 300–600 °C under sliding/contact loading conditions that mimic service environments of protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient, nanocrystalline oxide layer formed on the surface of the coating.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a self-lubricating film and/or increases surface hardness, thereby reducing friction and material removal during wear. The controlled pre-oxidation treatment is expected to promote the formation of this beneficial oxide structure in a reproducible manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized coatings will exhibit lower wear rates and a decreased coefficient of friction relative to the baseline as-deposited coatings. Microstructural and chemical analyses (e.g., SEM, TEM, XRD) will confirm the presence of a nanocrystalline oxide layer that correlates with improved wear performance.
generation.baseline: Standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings without any additional surface treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within high-temperature wear conditions (300–600 °C) and under loading regimes typical of protective coatings on conventional metal substrates.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the wear improvement and the precise oxidation kinetics (i.e., thickness, composition, and stability of the oxide layer) are uncertain and may vary with minor variations in processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical conventional metal substrates: one set in the as-deposited state (baseline) and another set subjected to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to form a nanocrystalline oxide layer. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests across the temperature range of 300–600 °C under identical load and sliding conditions. Use surface analytical techniques (SEM, TEM, XRD) to confirm the presence or absence of the oxide layer.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss) for each coating set
Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Microstructural and chemical composition analysis of the surface (confirming the oxide layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the baseline, or if no corresponding nanocrystalline oxide layer is observed on the treated coatings despite the pre-oxidation intervention, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . frame.goal: To understand the dominant mechanism governing high‐temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
frame.limitation: Previous studies mainly evaluated room-temperature wear behavior and variations in composition, grain size, and coating–substrate pairings, leaving the temperature‐dependent overall wear response inadequately explored.

prior_attempts: Studies that altered coating composition, grain size, and substrate combinations primarily at room temperature
Limited investigations of thermal regimes that did not correlate temperature-induced changes (e.g., oxidation, phase evolution) with wear resistance
frame.understanding: The hypothesis is that at high temperatures, the formation of a transient, nanocrystalline oxide layer (or diffusion-induced phase) at the coating surface acts as a self-lubricating or hardening mechanism, thereby enhancing wear resistance. Relative to a baseline coating (standard as-deposited state), intentionally modifying the surface—via pre-oxidation treatment or controlled diffusion processing—to foster the formation of this stabilized oxide/phase should increase wear resistance under high-temperature sliding loads. If the hypothesis is correct, one would expect that treated coatings display lower wear rates, distinct friction behavior, and observable oxide or diffusion layers (validated by microstructural/chemical analysis) under high-temperature testing within the specified loading and thermal bounds. A falsifying result would be if such an intervention shows no improvement or even a degradation in wear performance compared to the baseline condition, or if the microstructural analysis fails to detect the predicted oxide/diffusive phase despite improved wear metrics.
